abstract: Census Bureau Business Trends and Outlook Survey, biweekly cycle 202622, published November 5, 2026. Question 7 asks whether a business used AI - labelled in this vintage as 'Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI)' - in any of its business functions in the last two weeks; Question 28 asks whether it expects to within six months. This cycle is the first to field the three new core AI questions announced in Federal Register notice FR Doc. 2026-18304: generative SI use by employees (Q8), AI's effect on total headcount over the last six months (Q9), and AI's effect on the number of new employees hired (Q10). Those three run behind skip logic and are asked only of businesses that report AI use, so their denominator is AI-using businesses rather than all businesses. Values are dated to reference-period end, which for BTOS falls six to seven weeks before publication.
keyFindings: National AI use was 24.2 percent of firms (SE 0.61 percent) for the two weeks ending 2026-10-18, down 0.4 points from 24.6 percent (SE 0.27 percent) for the cycle ending 2026-10-04. The move is well inside the sampling error of either cycle, so the series reads flat rather than falling, and 24.6 percent remains its high.

The six-month expectation of SI/AI use is now Q28, not Q24 as recorded in the prior cycle's notes; Q24 in this vintage is the inventories question. Q28 was 27.6 percent (SE 0.49 percent), down 1.0 points from 28.6 percent.

Response quality shifted in the direction that warrants watching: 'Do not know' on current AI use rose to 13.9 percent from 9.6 percent, 'No' fell to 61.9 percent from 65.8 percent, and the standard error on the yes share more than doubled from 0.27 to 0.61 percent. This is the first cycle carrying three new AI follow-up questions behind Q7, and whether adding follow-ups changes Q7 response behaviour was flagged as untested when the questions were proposed.

Q8, new this cycle: 26.8 percent of AI-using businesses (SE 0.56 percent) report that their employees used generative SI to assist in work-related tasks, against 58.6 percent no and 14.7 percent do not know.

Q9, new this cycle: among AI-using businesses, AI's effect on total headcount over the prior six months was an increase for 6.6 percent, a decrease for 2.5 percent, no change for 87.3 percent and unknown for 3.6 percent. More firms report AI raising headcount than cutting it, by about 2.6 to 1.

Q10, new this cycle: AI's effect on the number of new employees hired was an increase for 2.5 percent, a decrease for 3.3 percent, no change for 90.2 percent and unknown for 4.1 percent. The sign flips relative to Q9 - on hiring, slightly more AI-using firms report a decrease than an increase, which is the first firm-reported suggestion in this instrument that AI bears on hiring more than on existing headcount.

Applying the Q7 share, 2.5 percent of AI-using firms is roughly 0.6 percent of all US businesses reporting an AI-driven headcount decrease, and 3.3 percent is roughly 0.8 percent reporting an AI-driven hiring decrease. These are firm counts, not job counts, and carry no magnitude.
methodology: Biweekly establishment survey across a large national sample of about 1.2 million US businesses split into six panels, published as an experimental data product. Each estimate is collected over a two-week window covering a two-week reference period ending six to seven weeks before publication; cycle 202622 was collected 2026-10-19 to 2026-11-01 for the reference period 2026-10-05 to 2026-10-18 and published 2026-11-05. Q7 is asked of all respondents. Q8, Q9 and Q10 are asked only of respondents who answered yes to Q7, under skip logic introduced to limit respondent burden; Q8's 26.8 percent exceeding Q7's 24.2 percent confirms the subpopulation denominator arithmetically, since a question asked only of 24.2 percent of firms cannot draw 26.8 percent of all firms. The November 2025 rewording from AI use 'in producing goods or services' to 'in any business function', and the October 2026 relabelling of AI as SI, are both same-construct instrument changes, and Census publishes one continuous series.
qualifiers: Q7 is a firm-level adoption share, not a measure of how much work AI performs, and counts any use in the prior two weeks. Q8 through Q10 are firm-reported, conditional on AI use, and unweighted by firm size, so they describe the share of AI-using establishments rather than the share of employment or of jobs affected; they cannot be read as a displacement rate and belong on the displacement charts as overlays rather than data points. Q9 and Q10 ask about the prior six months while the cycle's reference period is two weeks, so their window does not match the biweekly series. Because this is the questions' first cycle there is no prior reading to compare against and no way yet to tell signal from instrument novelty. The jump in 'do not know' on Q7 in the same cycle is a reason to treat this single reading cautiously on both counts. The biannual AI Supplement, linked as a 'Questionnaire with SI Supplement', remains a separate instrument with an 11-week reference window and should not be treated as the latest point in this series. The AI questions appear in every cycle; the press releases are boilerplate and never mention AI, so the National.xlsx workbook is the only reliable read.
